source_text: Μέθη, ὁ αὐθαίρετος δαίμων, ἐξ ἡδονῆς ταῖς ψυχαῖς ἐμβαλλόμενος, μέθη, κακίας μήτηρ, ἀρετῆς ἐναντίωσις, τὸν ἀνδρεῖον δειλὸν ἀποδείκνυσι, τὸν σώφρονα ἀσελγῆ· δικαιοσύνην οὐκ οἶδε, φρόνησιν ἀναιρεῖ. Ὥσπερ γὰρ ὕδωρ πολέμιόν ἐστι πυρὶ, οὕ τως ἀμετρία οἴνου λογισμὸν κατασβέννυσι. Διό περ ὤκνουν τι λέγειν κατὰ μέθης, οὐχ ὡς περὶ μικροῦ τινος κακοῦ ἢ παροφθῆναι ἀξίου, ἀλλ' ὡς οὐδὲν ὄφελος παρεχομένου τοῦ λόγου. Εἰ γὰρ ὁ μεθύων παραφρονεῖ καὶ ἐσκότωται, εἰκῆ ῥαψῳδεῖ ὁ ἐπιπλήττων τῷ μὴ ἀκούοντι. Τίσιν οὖν διαλεχθῶμεν; εἴπερ ὁ μὲν χρῄζων τῆς παραινέσεως οὐκ ἀκούει τῶν λεγο μένων· ὁ δὲ σωφρονῶν καὶ νήφων οὐ δεῖται τῆς ἐκ τοῦ λόγου βοηθείας, καθαρεύων τοῦ πάθους. Τί οὖν χρήσομαι τοῖς παροῦσιν, εἰ καὶ ὁ λόγος ἄχρη στος, καὶ ἡ σιωπὴ ἄπορος; Παρίδωμεν τὴν ἐπιμέ λειαν; Ἀλλ' ἐπικίνδυνος ἡ ἀμέλεια. Ἀλλὰ φθέγξομαί τι κατὰ τῶν μεθυόντων; Ἀλλ' εἰς νεκρὰς ἀκοὰς ἐνηχοῦμεν. Μήποτε οὖν, ὡς ἐπὶ τῶν λοιμικῶν νοση μάτων οἱ τῶν σωμάτων θεραπευταὶ τοὺς μὲν ὑγιαίνοντας τοῖς προφυλακτικοῖς βοηθήμασιν ἀσφαλίζον ται, τοῖς δὲ κεκρατημένοις ὑπὸ τοῦ πάθους οὐκ ἐγχειροῦσιν· οὕτω καὶ ὑμῖν ἐξ ἡμισείας ἔχει ὁ λόγος τὸ χρήσιμον· φυλακὴν ὑποδεικνὺς τοῖς ἀπα θέσιν, οὐκ ἀπαλλαγὴν καὶ ἴασιν τοῖς ὑπὸ τοῦ πάθους κεκρατημένοις. Τίνι διενήνοχας τῶν ἀλόγων, ὦ ἄνθρωπε; Οὐ τῇ δωρεᾷ τοῦ λόγου, ἣν λαβὼν παρὰ τοῦ κτίσαντός σε, ἄρχων καὶ κύριος ἐγένου πάσης τῆς κτίσεως; Ὁ τοίνυν ἀφελόμενος ἑαυτοῦ τὴν φρόνησιν διὰ τῆς μέ θης, Παρασυνεβλήθη τοῖς κτήνεσι τοῖς ἀνοήτοις, καὶ ὡμοιώθη αὐτοῖς. Μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ τῶν βοσκημά των φαίην ἂν ἔγωγε ἀλογωτέρους εἶναι τοὺς ἐν τῇ μέθῃ· εἴπερ τὰ μὲν τετράποδα πάντα καὶ τὰ θηρία τεταγμένας ἔχει τὰς πρὸς τὴν μίξιν ὁρμὰς, οἱ δὲ ὑπὸ τῆς μέθης τὴν ψυχὴν κατεχόμενοι, καὶ τὸ σῶμα τῆς παρὰ φύσιν θερμότητος ἀναπλήσαντες, πάντα καιρὸν καὶ πᾶσαν ὥραν πρὸς τὰς ἀκαθάρτους καὶ ἀσχήμονας συμπλοκὰς καὶ ἡδονὰς συνελαύνον ται. Καὶ οὐ τοῦτο μόνον τὴν ἀλογίαν αὐτοῖς ἐμποιεῖ, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ τῶν αἰσθήσεων παρατροπὴ χείρονα παν τὸς κτήνους ἀποδείκνυσι τὸν μεθύοντα. Ποῖον γὰρ βόσκημα οὕτω παραβλέπει καὶ οὕτω παρακούει ὡς ὁ μεθύων; Οὐκ ἀγνοοῦσι μὲν τοὺς οἰκειοτάτους, προστρέχουσι δὲ πολλάκις τοῖς ἀλλοτρίοις ὡς τοῖς συνήθεσιν; Οὐ τὰς σκιὰς διαπηδῶσι πολλάκις ὡς ὀχετοὺς ἢ φάραγγας; Ἤχων δὲ αὐτοῖς καὶ ψόφων, οἱονεὶ θαλάσσης κυμαινούσης, τὰ ὦτα πεπλήρωται· ἡ δὲ γῆ πρὸς τὸ ὄρθιον διανίστασθαι δοκεῖ, καὶ τὰ ὄρη περιτρέχειν ἐν κύκλῳ. Οὗτοι ποτὲ μὲν γελῶσιν ἄπαυστα, ποτὲ δὲ ὀδυνῶνται καὶ κλαίουσιν ἀπαρηγόρητα. Καὶ νῦν μὲν θρασεῖς εἰσι καὶ ἀπτόητοι, νῦν δὲ κατάφοβοι καὶ δειλοί. Τούτοις ὕπνοι μὲν βαρεῖς καὶ δυσανάφοροι καὶ πνιγώδεις, καὶ τῷ ὄντι θανάτου γείτονες, αἱ δὲ γρηγορήσεις τῶν ὕπνων ἀναισθητότεραι. Ἐνύπνιον γὰρ αὐτοῖς ἐστιν ὁ βίος, οἵ γε, ἱμάτιον οὐκ ἔχοντες, οὐδὲ τί φάγωσιν εἰς τὴν αὔριον, βασιλεύουσι καὶ στρατοπέδων ἄρχου σιν ἐν τῇ μέθῃ, καὶ πόλεις οἰκοδομοῦσι, καὶ χρή ματα διανέμουσι. Τοιούτων φαντασιῶν καὶ ἀπάτης τοσαύτης περιζέων ὁ οἶνος τὰς καρδίας αὐτῶν πλη ροῖ.
thought_title: Drunkenness as voluntary demon and its effects
orientation: Basil is lamenting the drunkenness that undid his Lenten exhortations, and now he begins to describe drunkenness itself as a voluntary demon that destroys reason and makes people worse than animals.
pass_a_gloss: Drunkenness, the self-chosen demon, throwing itself into souls from pleasure, drunkenness, mother of vice, opposition of virtue, makes the brave man cowardly, the self-controlled man licentious; it does not know righteousness, it destroys prudence. For just as water is hostile to fire, so excess of wine extinguishes reason. Therefore I was hesitating to say anything against drunkenness, not as about some small evil or one worthy to be overlooked, but as the word providing no benefit. For if the drunkard is deranged and darkened, in vain does the one rebuking the one not hearing sing rhapsodies. To whom then shall we speak? since the one needing the exhortation does not hear the things being said; but the one being self-controlled and sober does not need the help from the word, being clean of the passion. What then shall I do with those present, if both the word is useless, and silence is without resource? Shall we neglect the care? But negligence is dangerous. But shall I utter something against the drunkards? But we sound into dead ears. Perhaps then, just as in the case of pestilential diseases the healers of bodies secure the healthy ones with preventive remedies, but do not operate on those overcome by the disease; so also for you the word has its usefulness by half; showing protection to those without the passion, not deliverance and healing to those overcome by the passion. In what have you differed from the irrational animals, O man? Not in the gift of reason, which having received from the one who created you, you became ruler and lord of all creation? The one therefore who has taken away from himself his prudence through drunkenness, has been compared to the senseless beasts, and has been made like them. But rather I myself would say that those in drunkenness are more irrational than even the grazing animals; since all the four-footed animals and the wild beasts have ordered impulses toward mating, but those whose soul is held fast by drunkenness, and who have filled the body with unnatural heat, are driven together toward unclean and shameful entanglements and pleasures at every season and every hour. And not only this produces irrationality in them, but also the perversion of the senses shows the drunkard to be worse than every beast. For what grazing animal looks askance and hears amiss as the drunkard does? Do they not fail to recognize their dearest ones, and often run up to strangers as to their acquaintances? Do they not often leap over shadows as over channels or ravines? And their ears are filled with echoes and noises, as of a sea swelling with waves; and the earth seems to rise up to the height, and the mountains to run around in a circle. These men sometimes laugh unceasingly, and sometimes are in pain and weep inconsolably. And now they are bold and fearless, and now terrified and cowardly. For these men sleeps are heavy and hard to rouse from and suffocating, and in truth neighbors of death, and their wakings are more insensible than their sleeps. For life is a dream to them, who, not having a cloak, nor what they may eat for tomorrow, are kings and command armies in drunkenness, and build cities, and distribute money. Seething with such fantasies and so much deception, wine fills their hearts.

choices.why: αὐθαίρετος means 'self-chosen' or 'voluntary'; Basil's point is that drunkenness is a demon people choose for themselves, not one imposed from outside

choices.english: throwing itself into souls from pleasure
choices.why: ἐμβαλλόμενος is middle voice, meaning the demon throws itself or bursts in; the pleasure is the source or starting point of the assault
ἐναντίωσις is a strong abstract noun meaning 'opposition' or 'contrariety'; Basil is defining drunkenness as the very antithesis of virtue

choices.english: in vain does he sing rhapsodies
choices.why: ῥαψῳδεῖ literally means 'recites rhapsodies' or 'declaims'; Basil uses it ironically for pointless speech addressed to someone who cannot hear
ἐνηχοῦμεν means 'we sound into' or 'we make a sound in'; the image is of speaking into ears that are as good as dead

choices.term: ἐξ ἡμισείας ἔχει ὁ λόγος τὸ χρήσιμον
choices.english: the word has its usefulness by half
choices.why: ἐξ ἡμισείας means 'by half' or 'in half measure'; Basil says the word is only half useful because it helps the healthy but not the already overcome
rejected: the word has half its usefulness

bible_refs.note: Παρασυνεβλήθη τοῖς κτήνεσι τοῖς ἀνοήτοις, καὶ ὡμοιώθη αὐτοῖς

pass_b_english: Drunkenness is a self-chosen demon, intruding into souls through pleasure. Drunkenness is the mother of vice, the opposition of virtue. It shows the brave man as a coward and the self-controlled man as wanton. It does not know righteousness, and it destroys prudence. For just as water is hostile to fire, so an excess of wine extinguishes reason. This is why I hesitated to say anything against drunkenness—not because it is a small evil or one worth overlooking, but because the word offers no benefit. For if the drunkard is deranged and darkened, the one who rebukes someone who cannot hear talks nonsense in vain. To whom, then, should we speak? The one who needs the exhortation does not hear what is said, while the self-controlled and sober person does not need the word's help, being clean of the passion. What then shall I do with those present, if the word is useless and silence is without resource? Should we abandon the care? But neglect is dangerous. Should I speak something against the drunkards? But we sound into dead ears. Perhaps, then, just as in contagious diseases the healers of bodies secure the healthy with preventive remedies but do not treat those already overcome by the disease, so for you the word has its usefulness by half: it points out protection to those without the passion, but not deliverance and healing to those already overcome by it.

How do you differ from the irrational animals, O man? Is it not by the gift of reason, which you received from your Creator and by which you became ruler and lord of all creation? The one, then, who strips himself of prudence through drunkenness has been compared to the senseless beasts and has become like them (Psalm 49:12). Indeed, I would say that those in drunkenness are even more irrational than the grazing animals. For all four-footed creatures and wild beasts have fixed seasons for their impulses toward mating, but those whose souls are held fast by drunkenness, having filled their bodies with unnatural heat, are driven at every season and every hour toward unclean and shameful couplings and pleasures. And this is not the only thing that produces irrationality in them: the perversion of their senses also shows the drunkard to be worse than any beast. For what grazing animal completely fails to see and fails to hear as the drunkard does? Do they not recognize their dearest ones, yet often run up to strangers as if they were acquaintances? Do they not often leap over shadows as if they were ditches or ravines? Their ears are filled with echoes and noises as if a sea were swelling, while the earth seems to rise up steeply and the mountains to run around in a circle. Sometimes they laugh without stopping, and sometimes they suffer and weep without consolation. Now they are bold and fearless, now terrified and cowardly. Their sleep is heavy, hard to shake off, and suffocating—truly a neighbor of death—and their waking hours are more insensible than their sleep. For their life is a dream: though they have no cloak and nothing to eat for tomorrow, in their drunkenness they reign, command armies, build cities, and distribute riches. Wine, boiling over with such fantasies and so much deception, fills their hearts.

problems.quote: throwing itself into souls from pleasure
problems.why: Middle voice ἐμβαλλόμενος means 'thrusting itself in' or 'intruding,' not 'throwing itself from pleasure.' ἐξ ἡδονῆς means 'through pleasure' or 'by means of pleasure,' not 'from pleasure' as source.
problems.fix: a demon that intrudes into souls through pleasure
problems.ruling: ἐξ ἡδονῆς means 'from/through pleasure,' not 'from pleasure' in sense of origin; ἐμβαλλόμενος is 'intruding upon' souls

problems.why: ῥαψῳδεῖ here means 'speaks at random, talks nonsense' (LSJ II), not literally 'sings rhapsodies.' The point is futile speech, not poetic performance.
problems.ruling: ῥαψῳδεῖ here means 'talks nonsense' (LSJ II), not literal 'sings rhapsodies'; reader misled

problems.quote: but do not operate on those already overcome
problems.source_quote: τοῖς δὲ κεκρατημένοις ὑπὸ τοῦ πάθους οὐκ ἐγχειροῦσιν
problems.why: ἐγχειροῦσιν means 'lay hands on, treat, undertake,' not specifically 'operate on.' The medical metaphor is general treatment, not surgical operation.
problems.fix: but do not treat those already overcome
problems.ruling: ἐγχειροῦσιν means 'undertake/treat,' not 'operate on'; modern surgical connotation misleads reader

edits.old: throwing itself into souls from pleasure
but do not operate on those already overcome
edits.new: but do not treat those already overcome

fixed: ἐμβαλλόμενος is middle voice 'intruding/thrusting itself in'; ἐξ ἡδονῆς means 'through pleasure' as means, not source.
ῥαψῳδεῖ here means 'speaks at random, talks nonsense' (LSJ II), not literally 'sings rhapsodies.'
ἐγχειροῦσιν means 'lay hands on, treat, undertake,' not specifically 'operate on.'

problems.why: παρα- here intensifies to 'completely miss, fail to see/hear', not 'aside'.
problems.fix: so completely fails to see and fails to hear.
problems.ruling: παραβλέπει/παρακούει here means 'sees/hears amiss' (drunken misperception), not 'looks aside/hears aside'.

problems.quote: Do they not fail to recognize their dearest ones
problems.why: Misreads syntax: οὐκ ἀγνοοῦσι μὲν... προστρέχουσι δὲ = 'they don't fail to recognize... but run to strangers'.
problems.fix: Do they not recognize their dearest ones, yet often run to strangers as acquaintances?
problems.ruling: οὐκ ἀγνοοῦσι... προστρέχουσι δέ = 'they DO fail to recognize dearest ones but run to strangers.' English inverts the meaning.

edits.new: completely fails to see and fails to hear

edits.old: Do they not fail to recognize their dearest ones, and often run up to strangers as if they were acquaintances?
edits.new: Do they not recognize their dearest ones, yet often run up to strangers as if they were acquaintances?

fixed: παραβλέπει and παρακούει: παρα- intensifies to 'completely miss, fail to see/hear', so 'looks aside and hears aside' misstates the source; changed to 'completely fails to see and fails to hear'.

Οὐκ ἀγνοοῦσι μὲν... προστρέχουσι δὲ: the μὲν...δὲ contrast means they do recognize their dearest ones but run to strangers; changed to 'Do they not recognize their dearest ones, yet often run up to strangers as if they were acquaintances?'

last_rejected.why: First-person plural hides Basil's solitary struggle; Greek has singular.
last_rejected.fix: But I sound into dead ears.
last_rejected.ruling: ἐνηχοῦμεν is first-person plural in Greek; English correctly renders it 'we sound.'

last_rejected.why: Misreads genitive absolute as nominative; 'the word' is not subject but genitive.
last_rejected.fix: because speech offers no benefit / because my words would do no good.
last_rejected.ruling: τοῦ λόγου is genitive subject of παρεχομένου; 'the word offers no benefit' correctly renders it.

last_rejected.quote: so for you the word has its usefulness by half
last_rejected.source_quote: οὕτω καὶ ὑμῖν ἐξ ἡμισείας ἔχει ὁ λόγος τὸ χρήσιμον
last_rejected.why: Misreads dative; 'for you' should be 'for us' or 'in our case'—Basil includes himself.
last_rejected.fix: so in our case too the word has half its usefulness.
last_rejected.ruling: ὑμῖν is dative 'for you'; Basil addresses audience. 'For you' is correct, not 'for us.'

last_rejected.quote: Do they not recognize their dearest ones, yet often run up to strangers
last_rejected.source_quote: Οὐκ ἀγνοοῦσι μὲν τοὺς οἰκειοτάτους, προστρέχουσι δὲ πολλάκις τοῖς ἀλλοτρίοις ὡς τοῖς συνήθεσιν
last_rejected.why: Subject confusion: 'they' refers to drunkards, not animals; Greek asks if drunkards don't fail to recognize kin.
last_rejected.fix: Do they not fail to recognize their closest kin, yet often run to strangers as to familiars?
last_rejected.ruling: Context (Ποῖον βόσκημα... ὡς ὁ μεθύων) shows drunkards are subject throughout; English 'they' correctly refers to drunkards.

last_rejected.quote: Do they not often leap over shadows as if they were ditches or ravines
last_rejected.source_quote: Οὐ τὰς σκιὰς διαπηδῶσι πολλάκις ὡς ὀχετοὺς ἢ φάραγγας
last_rejected.why: Missing negative: 'Do they not' should be 'Do they not'—but Greek asks if they DON'T leap, i.e., they do leap.
last_rejected.fix: Do they not leap over shadows as if they were ditches or ravines?
last_rejected.ruling: Οὐ here is rhetorical 'surely they leap over shadows'; English 'Do they not often leap over' captures the same meaning.

last_rejected.quote: Their ears are filled with echoes and noises as if a sea were swelling
last_rejected.source_quote: Ἤχων δὲ αὐτοῖς καὶ ψόφων, οἱονεὶ θαλάσσης κυμαινούσης, τὰ ὦτα πεπλήρωται
last_rejected.why: Subject wrong: 'their ears' are filled, but 'as if a sea were swelling' should modify the noises, not be a separate clause.
last_rejected.fix: Their ears are filled with echoes and noises like a swelling sea.
last_rejected.ruling: English correctly states ears are filled with echoes/noises 'as if a sea were swelling'; a natural rendering of the comparison.

last_rejected.quote: the earth seems to rise up steeply and the mountains to run around in a circle
last_rejected.source_quote: ἡ δὲ γὴ πρὸς τὸ ὄρθιον διανίστασθαι δοκεῖ, καὶ τὰ ὄρη περιτρέχειν ἐν κύκλῳ
last_rejected.why: Missing subject: 'to them' or 'in their perception' needed; Greek has dative of experiencer.
last_rejected.fix: to them the earth seems to rise up steeply and the mountains to run around in a circle.
last_rejected.ruling: δοκεῖ 'seems' already implies perception; 'to them' is implicit. No meaning is lost in English.
